title: theory of obligation — general
content: Al-Sanhouri adopts the Roman-French classification while integrating Islamic jurisprudence. He treats obligation as having a dual nature: personal (tying the debtor) and proprietary (the creditor's enforceable right over the debtor's assets). The Egyptian Code enumerates five sources, with contract being primary. Al-Sanhouri emphasizes that the obligation's material/financial element is central to its identity and distinguishes civil obligations from natural obligations.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Obligation is a legal bond between creditor and debtor; debtor must perform or bear compulsory execution.
Sources of obligation under the Egyptian Civil Code: contract, unilateral will, tortious act, unjust enrichment, and law.
Obligation has two elements: personal element (debitum) binding the debtor, and proprietary element (obligatio) conferring execution right on the creditor.
Financial assessability of the object is essential to constitute a civil obligation.

sanhouri_position.short: Obligation is a personal right creating a legal bond. Its sources are enumerated in the Code; each source has distinct formation rules and effects.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri adopts the Roman-French classification while integrating Islamic jurisprudence. He treats obligation as having a dual nature: personal (tying the debtor) and proprietary (the creditor's enforceable right over the debtor's assets). The Egyptian Code enumerates five sources, with contract being primary. Al-Sanhouri emphasizes that the obligation's material/financial element is central to its identity and distinguishes civil obligations from natural obligations.

conditions: Obligation must have a legally recognized source.
Performance must be financially assessable or connected to a financially assessable interest.
Subject matter must be determinable.
exceptions: Natural obligations (الالتزام الطبيعي) are not judicially enforceable but voluntary performance is valid and irrecoverable.
effects: Creditor acquires right to compulsory execution against debtor's assets.
Debtor's entire estate is the general guarantee of all creditors.
Non-performance triggers liability for compensation.
common_disputes: Whether a natural obligation can be converted into a civil obligation by acknowledgment or novation.
Identifying the applicable source when facts overlap multiple categories.
practical_examples: Debt prescribed by limitation becomes natural obligation; voluntary payment is valid and irrecoverable.
Moral duty to support a relative beyond legal requirement is a natural obligation.

title: contract formation — offer and acceptance
content: Al-Sanhouri analyzes offer and acceptance under the will theory, requiring genuine matching intent. For absent parties, the Egyptian Code (Art. 98) adopts the receipt theory (نظرية العلم), not the dispatch theory, meaning formation occurs when acceptance reaches the offeror. Al-Sanhouri distinguishes offer to a specific person (lapses on death/incapacity before acceptance) from open offer to the public. An offer with a fixed time-limit is irrevocable within that period.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Contract is formed by matching offer and acceptance reflecting the parties' genuine intent.
Offer must be definite, complete on essential elements, and show intent to be bound.
Acceptance must match offer exactly; any modification constitutes a counter-offer.
Contract between absent parties is formed at the moment and place acceptance reaches the offeror (receipt theory — نظرية العلم).

sanhouri_position.short: Contract requires matching intent (offer + acceptance). Egyptian law adopts the receipt theory for distant contracts; formation occurs when and where acceptance is received by the offeror.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri analyzes offer and acceptance under the will theory, requiring genuine matching intent. For absent parties, the Egyptian Code (Art. 98) adopts the receipt theory (نظرية العلم), not the dispatch theory, meaning formation occurs when acceptance reaches the offeror. Al-Sanhouri distinguishes offer to a specific person (lapses on death/incapacity before acceptance) from open offer to the public. An offer with a fixed time-limit is irrevocable within that period.

conditions: Offer must be definite, complete on all essential terms, and indicate intent to be bound.
Acceptance must be unconditional and conform exactly to offer (mirror image rule).
Both parties must have legal capacity.
For absent parties: acceptance must reach offeror while offer still subsists.
exceptions: Silence constitutes acceptance only where law, custom, or prior dealings so provide.
Acceptance by conduct is valid where circumstances clearly indicate assent.
Death or incapacity of offeror before acceptance may lapse the offer depending on contract nature.
effects: Contract becomes binding on both parties from moment of formation.
Obligations arise immediately upon formation.
Place of formation governs jurisdiction and applicable law for absent-party contracts.
common_disputes: Time and place of formation between absent parties — key for jurisdiction.
Whether silence amounts to acceptance in commercial relationships.
Revocation of offer after acceptance dispatched.
Whether modified acceptance is counter-offer or valid acceptance.
practical_examples: Postal contract: binding when acceptance letter received by offeror, not when posted.
Online acceptance: binding when server receives the acceptance message.

title: legal capacity to contract (الأهلية)
content: Al-Sanhouri treats capacity as a condition extrinsic to consent. The Code distinguishes full incapacity (child below 7, insane person) producing void contracts, from relative incapacity (minor 7–18, partially incapacitated) producing voidable contracts. The distinction between purely beneficial, purely harmful, and mixed acts determines validity for minors. Protection is personal to the incapacitated party and their heirs.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Full legal capacity (أهلية كاملة) requires attaining majority (18 years) and soundness of mind.
Contracts by those with absolute incapacity are void; by those with relative incapacity are voidable.
Minor's purely beneficial acts are valid; purely harmful acts are void; mixed acts are voidable.
Discernment age (سن التمييز) is 7 years — below which all acts are absolutely void.

sanhouri_position.short: Capacity is presumed; incapacity is exceptional. Absolute incapacity renders contract void; relative incapacity renders it voidable for protection of the incapacitated party only.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri treats capacity as a condition extrinsic to consent. The Code distinguishes full incapacity (child below 7, insane person) producing void contracts, from relative incapacity (minor 7–18, partially incapacitated) producing voidable contracts. The distinction between purely beneficial, purely harmful, and mixed acts determines validity for minors. Protection is personal to the incapacitated party and their heirs.

conditions: Full capacity: age 18+, sound mind, not legally interdicted.
Guardian or court authorization required for acts beyond daily administration for ward.
Emancipation (تمكين) possible before 18 by court order.
exceptions: Minor's purely beneficial acts (unconditional gift acceptance) are valid without guardian approval.
Minor who conceals incapacity by fraud cannot invoke incapacity to annul contract.
effects: Void contract: no legal existence from inception; cannot be ratified.
Voidable contract: valid until annulled; ratification upon reaching capacity is effective.
Third parties acting in good faith with apparent representative may be protected.
common_disputes: Whether act is purely beneficial, purely harmful, or mixed.
Guardian acting ultra vires — court authorization requirement.
Emancipated minor's scope of contractual capacity.
practical_examples: Minor selling inherited property without guardian approval: voidable, not void.
Minor accepting unconditional gift: valid without guardian.

title: consent defect — mistake (غلط)
content: Al-Sanhouri adopts the objective-subjective standard: the substance of the thing means the essential quality that the parties considered decisive — assessed by the subjective intent of the mistaken party, bounded by the objective knowledge of the other. He rejects pure subjective theory. Mistake of law is treated equally with mistake of fact. The Egyptian Code innovates by requiring that the other party knew or should have known of the mistake, protecting good faith and commercial security.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Actionable mistake must be substantial: relating to the substance of the thing or a quality considered essential by the parties.
Mistake must be determinative — party would not have contracted but for it.
Other party must have known or should have known of the mistake.
Mistake of law is actionable on equal terms with mistake of fact under the Egyptian Code.

sanhouri_position.short: Actionable mistake must be substantial (relating to the thing's identity or principal quality) and known or knowable by the other party. Mistake in motive alone is insufficient.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri adopts the objective-subjective standard: the substance of the thing means the essential quality that the parties considered decisive — assessed by the subjective intent of the mistaken party, bounded by the objective knowledge of the other. He rejects pure subjective theory. Mistake of law is treated equally with mistake of fact. The Egyptian Code innovates by requiring that the other party knew or should have known of the mistake, protecting good faith and commercial security.

conditions: Mistake must relate to substance of thing (ذاتية الشيء) or quality considered essential.
Mistake must be determinative — party would not have contracted without it.
Other party must have known or should have known of the mistake.
Cannot invoke mistake if other party offers to perform as originally understood.
exceptions: Mistake in motive only does not give right to annul.
Mutual mistake — both parties share same mistake — may give right to annul.
Gross negligence of mistaken party causing the mistake may lead court to deny annulment.
effects: Contract is voidable (قابل للإبطال) at instance of mistaken party only.
Court may award compensation to other party who suffered from annulment in good faith.
common_disputes: Whether quality is 'substantial' — subjective or objective assessment.
Mistake in identity of person vs. mistake in legal characterization.
Mistake in calculating price vs. mistake in the price itself.
practical_examples: Buyer mistakes bronze statue for gold: mistake in substance — voidable.
Party mistakes legal effect of contract terms: mistake of law — actionable.

title: consent defect — fraud (تدليس)
content: Al-Sanhouri defines fraud broadly to include positive misrepresentation and fraudulent concealment (تدليس بالكتمان). Fraud must be causative. He distinguishes fraud from lawful commercial puffery. Third-party fraud is actionable if the contracting party knew or should have known. Article 125(2) gross fraud (تدليس جسيم) allows annulment even if not absolutely determinative of consent. Annulment and tort damages may be pursued simultaneously or alternatively.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Fraud is deceptive means (acts, words, or fraudulent omission) by one party inducing the other to contract.
Fraudulent concealment of information the other party was duty-bound to disclose is actionable.
No requirement that fraud relate to substance — any determinative deception suffices.
Fraud by third party with the contracting party's knowledge also vitiates consent.

sanhouri_position.short: Fraud requires: deceptive act or omission by contracting party (or third party with their knowledge), causing consent. Gross fraud permits annulment even without absolute determinativeness. Fraud always grounds tort damages.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri defines fraud broadly to include positive misrepresentation and fraudulent concealment (تدليس بالكتمان). Fraud must be causative. He distinguishes fraud from lawful commercial puffery. Third-party fraud is actionable if the contracting party knew or should have known. Article 125(2) gross fraud (تدليس جسيم) allows annulment even if not absolutely determinative of consent. Annulment and tort damages may be pursued simultaneously or alternatively.

conditions: Deceptive means: act, words, or fraudulent concealment.
Deception from the other contracting party or third party with their knowledge.
Must be determinative: party would not have contracted but for the fraud.
Fraudulent intent (قصد التضليل) must exist.
exceptions: Fraud by third party without contracting party's knowledge: annulment denied; tort damages only.
Customary trade exaggeration (مبالغة تجارية معتادة) is not fraud.
Non-disclosure without duty to disclose: generally not actionable fraud.
effects: Contract is voidable at instance of defrauded party.
Defrauded party may claim tort damages independently of or in addition to annulment.
Annulment is retroactive; restitution obligations arise.
common_disputes: Distinguishing actionable fraudulent concealment from permissible silence.
Fraud by agent or broker — imputed to principal.
Whether commercial optimism amounts to fraud.
practical_examples: Seller conceals known structural defect in building: fraudulent omission — voidable + damages.
Party misrepresents financial solvency to induce credit: fraud — voidable.

title: consent defect — coercion/duress (إكراه)
content: Al-Sanhouri introduces undue moral influence (النفوذ الأدبي) as a statutory category of coercion under Article 129. Unlike the French Code, Egyptian law expressly covers domination through authority, trust, or psychological subjugation. The subjective test asks: did this person actually lose free will? Coercion differs from fraud: no requirement that it originate from the other party — any coercion by anyone vitiates consent. Lawful threats are excluded: creditor threatening to sue on a legitimate debt is not coercion.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Coercion vitiates consent when a party is threatened with serious, imminent, unlawful harm.
Threat must deprive party of free will; standard is subjective — accounting for person's age, sex, health, social position.
Undue moral influence (النفوذ الأدبي) is expressly assimilated to coercion when it destroys free will.
Coercion by any third party (even unknown to contracting party) still gives right to annul.

sanhouri_position.short: Al-Sanhouri's major innovation: inclusion of moral undue influence under Art. 129. Subjective test. Third-party coercion always permits annulment — unlike fraud. Lawful threat (e.g., filing a legitimate suit) is not coercion.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri introduces undue moral influence (النفوذ الأدبي) as a statutory category of coercion under Article 129. Unlike the French Code, Egyptian law expressly covers domination through authority, trust, or psychological subjugation. The subjective test asks: did this person actually lose free will? Coercion differs from fraud: no requirement that it originate from the other party — any coercion by anyone vitiates consent. Lawful threats are excluded: creditor threatening to sue on a legitimate debt is not coercion.

conditions: Threat of serious harm: to life, body, honor, or property of party or close relative.
Threat must be imminent and not contingent on remote uncertain events.
Threat must be unlawful.
Causal link: coercion induced the contract.
For moral influence: relationship of authority/trust exploiting psychological subjugation.
exceptions: Lawful threat (creditor threatening suit for legitimate debt) is not coercion.
General fear without identifiable person exerting it: not coercion.
Coercion must actually cause consent — if party would have contracted anyway: no annulment.
effects: Contract is voidable at instance of coerced party.
Independent right to claim damages.
Third-party coercion: voidable regardless of whether other party knew.
common_disputes: Whether economic necessity/financial duress constitutes coercion.
Undue moral influence in family, religious, or employer-employee relationships.
Distinguishing normal commercial pressure from unlawful coercion.
practical_examples: Employer threatening dismissal to compel unfavorable waiver: potential undue moral influence.
Creditor threatening criminal complaint to coerce settlement on unlawful claim: coercion.

title: lesion and exploitation (غبن واستغلال)
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes Egyptian law from French (which rejects general lesion) and Islamic law (which recognizes pure lesion). Article 129 requires both elements cumulatively: material imbalance and exploitation of vulnerability. This reflects the Egyptian Code's social-solidaristic approach influenced by Islamic prohibition of exploitation (أكل أموال الناس بالباطل). The court's primary power is to adjust, not void.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Lesion alone (simple disproportion) does not vitiate contract in Egyptian law.
Actionable lesion requires: objective imbalance + exploitation of need, recklessness, or inexperience.
Primary remedy is judicial reduction/adjustment of obligations, not annulment.
One-year limitation period from contract date.

sanhouri_position.short: Egyptian law adopts qualified lesion: requires both objective disproportion and subjective exploitation. Pure market disproportion is insufficient. Remedy is reduction/equalization first; annulment only if equalization impossible.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes Egyptian law from French (which rejects general lesion) and Islamic law (which recognizes pure lesion). Article 129 requires both elements cumulatively: material imbalance and exploitation of vulnerability. This reflects the Egyptian Code's social-solidaristic approach influenced by Islamic prohibition of exploitation (أكل أموال الناس بالباطل). The court's primary power is to adjust, not void.

conditions: Objective: serious disproportion between the two performances.
Subjective: exploitation of victim's financial need, recklessness (رعونة), or inexperience.
Both conditions must coexist at time of contracting.
Claim within one year of contract.
exceptions: Post-contract change in values does not create lesion retrospectively.
Arm's length commercial transaction between experienced parties — disproportion alone irrelevant.
effects: Court may reduce excessive obligations or increase deficient counter-performance.
If equalization impossible: court may annul contract.
Prescription: one year from contract.
common_disputes: Threshold of 'serious' disproportion — no fixed percentage in law.
Proving exploitation of weakness — evidentiary burden on claimant.
Interaction with usury rules in loan contracts.
practical_examples: Farmer in acute financial distress selling land far below market: exploitation — adjustment.
Inexperienced heir induced to waive inheritance share grossly below value: lesion + exploitation.

title: contract object — محل العقد
content: Al-Sanhouri treats the object of contract as distinct from the object of obligation. Each obligation's object must satisfy four conditions. On impossibility: only original absolute impossibility voids the contract; supervening impossibility triggers force majeure. On determinacy: genus obligations require at minimum kind and quantity. Unlawfulness of object (violating public order or morals) produces absolute nullity, not mere voidability — this is non-waivable.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Object must be: possible, determinable, lawful, and in commerce (قابل للتعامل).
Future things may be subject matter; sale of another person's living inheritance is void.
Object must be determinable — specific, or determinable by genus and quantity.
Unlawful object (contrary to public order or morals) renders contract absolutely void.

sanhouri_position.short: Object (محل الالتزام) is what the debtor must give, do, or refrain from. It must be possible, determinable, lawful, and tradeable. Future things are valid subject matter. Unlawfulness of object produces absolute nullity.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri treats the object of contract as distinct from the object of obligation. Each obligation's object must satisfy four conditions. On impossibility: only original absolute impossibility voids the contract; supervening impossibility triggers force majeure. On determinacy: genus obligations require at minimum kind and quantity. Unlawfulness of object (violating public order or morals) produces absolute nullity, not mere voidability — this is non-waivable.

conditions: Possible: not absolutely impossible at time of contracting.
Determinable: identified specifically or by kind/quality/quantity.
Lawful: not contrary to public order (النظام العام) or public morals (الآداب العامة).
In commerce: tradeable under law.
exceptions: Obligation to deliver a future thing is valid (sale of future harvest).
Sale of entirety of one's future estate is void.
Sale of inheritance of a living person: void (Article 131).
effects: Invalid object: contract is absolutely void (بطلان مطلق).
Partial invalidity of object: valid if severable from void part.
common_disputes: Whether partial illegality taints entire contract or only the unlawful clause.
Whether the object is sufficiently determinable.
Sale of disputed or uncertain future thing.
practical_examples: Agreement to sell human organs for profit: unlawful object — absolutely void.
Sale of next year's crop at fixed price: valid future-thing obligation.

title: contract cause — سبب العقد
content: Al-Sanhouri navigates between French cause theory and its critics. He treats cause in synallagmatic contracts as the counter-performance; in unilateral gratuitous acts as the liberality intent (نية التبرع). Innovation: where both parties share an unlawful motive, this infects the cause and voids the contract. Article 138 allows courts to void where cause (however stated) is actually unlawful. Al-Sanhouri argues cause theory serves as a check on contractual freedom in the public interest, drawing from Islamic prohibition of unlawful purposes.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Every obligation must have a cause; absence of cause or unlawful cause renders contract void.
Cause is presumed to exist and be lawful; burden of proof on party alleging otherwise.
In synallagmatic contracts: cause of each party's obligation is the other's counter-obligation.
Unlawful shared motive known to both parties voids contract on grounds of unlawful cause.

sanhouri_position.short: Al-Sanhouri adopts objective-causal theory with Islamic influence. In gratuitous acts, cause is the liberality intent (نية التبرع). Unlawful motive known to both parties infects cause and voids contract.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri navigates between French cause theory and its critics. He treats cause in synallagmatic contracts as the counter-performance; in unilateral gratuitous acts as the liberality intent (نية التبرع). Innovation: where both parties share an unlawful motive, this infects the cause and voids the contract. Article 138 allows courts to void where cause (however stated) is actually unlawful. Al-Sanhouri argues cause theory serves as a check on contractual freedom in the public interest, drawing from Islamic prohibition of unlawful purposes.

conditions: Cause must exist at time of contracting.
Cause must be lawful: not contrary to public order or morals.
In synallagmatic contracts: cause of each obligation is the other party's reciprocal obligation.
exceptions: Gratuitous acts are valid without counter-performance; cause is liberality intent.
Nominal (simulated) cause does not void contract if true cause is lawful.
Unilateral unlawful motive unknown to other party does not void contract.
effects: Absence of cause: contract void.
Unlawful cause: absolutely void (بطلان مطلق).
Failure of cause after formation: triggers rescission rules.
common_disputes: Distinguishing unlawful cause from unlawful personal motive.
Simulated contracts — true cause concealed.
Brokerage paid for securing unlawful transaction.
practical_examples: Payment to intermediary to bribe official: unlawful cause — void.
Apparent donation masking usurious loan: simulation — true cause examined.

title: absolute nullity — البطلان المطلق
content: Al-Sanhouri draws the fundamental distinction between absolute nullity (بطلان مطلق) and relative nullity (بطلان نسبي/إبطال). Absolute nullity protects general social interest; relative nullity protects private interest. Consequences differ: absolute nullity — no prescription, no ratification, invocable by all parties and court; relative nullity — prescribes in 3 years, only victim can invoke, ratification possible. He explicitly rejects a third 'non-existence' category — treating non-existence as the most severe form of absolute nullity.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Void contract (عقد باطل) has no legal existence from inception; produces no effects.
Absolute nullity protects the general interest (public order, morals); any person or court may invoke it ex officio.
Void contract cannot be ratified; no prescription validates it.
Court declares nullity ex officio without party request.

sanhouri_position.short: Absolute nullity arises from defects affecting public interest: missing essential element, unlawful object/cause, complete incapacity. Permanent, invocable by anyone, court may declare sua sponte. Egyptian law does not recognize 'non-existence' as a separate third category.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri draws the fundamental distinction between absolute nullity (بطلان مطلق) and relative nullity (بطلان نسبي/إبطال). Absolute nullity protects general social interest; relative nullity protects private interest. Consequences differ: absolute nullity — no prescription, no ratification, invocable by all parties and court; relative nullity — prescribes in 3 years, only victim can invoke, ratification possible. He explicitly rejects a third 'non-existence' category — treating non-existence as the most severe form of absolute nullity.

conditions: Missing essential element: no matching consent, no object, no cause.
Unlawful object or cause (contrary to public order or morals).
Complete incapacity of party (child below 7, insane person without discernment).
Formal requirement violated when formality is an essential condition (عقود شكلية).
exceptions: Partial nullity: void clause severed if contract remains viable without it.
Conversion (تحويل العقد): void contract may produce effects of a different valid legal act if its elements exist.
effects: No legal effect from inception.
Restitution of all performances exchanged.
Third parties who dealt in good faith may be protected under special rules (e.g., land registration).
common_disputes: Whether violation is of public order (absolute nullity) or private protection (relative nullity).
Extent of restitution obligation after nullity declaration.
Whether partial nullity taints the entire contract.
practical_examples: Contract for sale of narcotics: unlawful object — absolute nullity.
Contract by a person below 7: complete incapacity — absolute nullity.

title: relative nullity / annulment — البطلان النسبي (الإبطال)
content: Al-Sanhouri systematizes relative nullity around the principle of private protection. The contract exists and produces full effects until the protected party exercises the annulment right. Three-year limitation runs from: knowledge of mistake/fraud, cessation of coercion, or reaching majority. Ratification retroactively validates from formation. He emphasizes annulment operates between parties only; third parties who acquired rights in good faith are protected against retroactive effect.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Voidable contract is valid and produces full effects until annulled by the protected party only.
Grounds: relative incapacity, consent defects (mistake, fraud, coercion, lesion).
Right to annul prescribes in 3 years from discovery of defect or cessation of coercion.
Ratification (إجازة صريحة أو ضمنية) extinguishes right to annul retroactively.

sanhouri_position.short: Relative nullity protects private interest. Only the protected party may invoke it. Contract stands until judicially annulled. Ratification, express or implied by conduct, permanently validates the contract retroactively from inception.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri systematizes relative nullity around the principle of private protection. The contract exists and produces full effects until the protected party exercises the annulment right. Three-year limitation runs from: knowledge of mistake/fraud, cessation of coercion, or reaching majority. Ratification retroactively validates from formation. He emphasizes annulment operates between parties only; third parties who acquired rights in good faith are protected against retroactive effect.

conditions: Defect is one protecting private interest: consent defect or relative incapacity.
Annulment claimed within 3 years (from discovery, cessation of coercion, or majority).
No prior ratification (express or implied by conduct).
exceptions: Prescription does not begin to run until the defect is discoverable.
Third-party rights in good faith protected against retroactive annulment effects.
If both parties participated in the cause of nullity — in pari delicto rules may apply.
effects: Annulment retroactive to formation: restitution obligations arise.
Contracting party may claim damages if annulment caused loss.
Ratification: contract deemed fully valid from inception — irrevocable.
common_disputes: When 3-year prescription begins — date of knowledge vs. date of act.
Whether conduct amounts to implied ratification (e.g., partial performance after discovering defect).
Extent of restitution after annulment when performances have been partially consumed.
practical_examples: Minor who contracted under fraud: 3 years from reaching majority or discovering fraud, whichever later.
Party continues performing contract after discovering coercion has ceased: implied ratification.

title: binding force of contract — القوة الملزمة للعقد
content: Al-Sanhouri designed the Egyptian hardship doctrine (نظرية الظروف الطارئة) in Article 147/2, distinguishing it clearly from force majeure (which extinguishes the obligation entirely). Hardship makes performance excessively burdensome but not impossible. Four cumulative conditions must be met. The court's power is limited to reducing the exorbitant part to a reasonable level — not to annul the contract or create new terms. This reflects his social-contractual philosophy balancing individual autonomy with collective welfare, drawing from Islamic jurisprudence on changed circumstances.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: binding force of contract — القوة الملزمة للعقد
core_principles: Contract is the law of the parties: neither may unilaterally revoke or amend it.
Court cannot modify contract terms except as specifically permitted by law.
Good faith obligation attaches to performance and execution.
Hardship doctrine (نظرية الظروف الطارئة): court may reduce oppressive obligations if unforeseen general event makes performance catastrophically burdensome.

sanhouri_position.short: Binding force is the cornerstone of contracts. Al-Sanhouri is the primary architect of Egypt's hardship doctrine (Art. 147/2) — courts may reduce (not annul) obligations made catastrophic by unforeseen general events, balancing pacta sunt servanda with social justice.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri designed the Egyptian hardship doctrine (نظرية الظروف الطارئة) in Article 147/2, distinguishing it clearly from force majeure (which extinguishes the obligation entirely). Hardship makes performance excessively burdensome but not impossible. Four cumulative conditions must be met. The court's power is limited to reducing the exorbitant part to a reasonable level — not to annul the contract or create new terms. This reflects his social-contractual philosophy balancing individual autonomy with collective welfare, drawing from Islamic jurisprudence on changed circumstances.

conditions: Valid formed contract.

Hardship: (1) unforeseen general event after contracting; (2) performance excessively onerous (not impossible); (3) event not foreseeable at contracting; (4) event is general in nature, not personal to debtor.
exceptions: Parties may contractually exclude hardship relief in advance.
Hardship does not apply to already-completed obligations.
Personal financial difficulty of debtor alone is not a qualifying hardship event.
effects: Court reduces the exorbitant obligation to equitable level — not annulment.
Cannot increase counter-performance or impose new contractual terms.
If reduction insufficient: contract continues as-is.
common_disputes: Whether an economic crisis constitutes an unforeseen general event.
Distinguishing hardship (excessive burden) from force majeure (impossibility).
Whether currency devaluation qualifies as a hardship event.
practical_examples: Long-term supply contract; raw material tripled due to unforeseen war: possible hardship.
Contractor's costs tripled due to general extraordinary inflation: may qualify.

title: contract effects on third parties — أثر العقد في حق الغير
content: Al-Sanhouri treats the stipulation pour autrui (الاشتراط لمصلحة الغير) as the principal exception to privity. The third-party beneficiary's right vests from formation of the stipulation, not upon acceptance — acceptance only confirms it and prevents revocation. The stipulator may revoke before acceptance by the third party. He discusses insurance contracts as the primary practical example. He also distinguishes the third party's direct right from the indirect subrogation of creditors.

Insurance beneficiary's rights against insurer directly.

title: contract interpretation — تفسير العقد
content: Al-Sanhouri follows French interpretive tradition: text is primary; intent supplies meaning only where ambiguous. Courts must not rewrite contracts under guise of interpretation. The rule of interpretation against the drafter in adhesion contracts is a deliberate social-protection measure for weaker parties (consumers, insureds). Good faith (Article 148) creates implied performance obligations derived from law, custom, and justice — supplementing express terms without overriding them.

core_principles: Clear contract text is applied as written; no interpretation of unambiguous text is permissible.

Customs and practices supplement contract terms as implied content.
Ambiguous clauses in adhesion contracts (عقود إذعان) interpreted against the drafting party.

sanhouri_position.short: Interpretation uncovers common intent. Clear text is final. Adhesion contract ambiguity resolved against stronger drafting party — a deliberate social-protection rule. Good faith fills performance gaps through implied terms from law, custom, and justice.

title: rescission for non-performance — الفسخ
content: Al-Sanhouri explains that Egyptian law (Art. 157) adopts the implied resolutory condition from Roman/French law but requires judicial intervention as default. The creditor cannot unilaterally rescind without court judgment unless a valid rescission clause exists. Court has wide discretion to deny rescission if breach is minor. A contractual rescission clause (شرط الفسخ الاتفاقي) operates automatically on breach but court still verifies the breach. Prior notice (إعذار) is required in most cases.

core_principles: In synallagmatic contracts, non-performance by one party entitles the other to seek rescission.

Contractual rescission clauses (شرط الفسخ الاتفاقي) are valid; court still verifies breach occurred.
Partial/minor non-performance does not justify total rescission.

sanhouri_position.short: Rescission is the implied resolutory condition in synallagmatic contracts. Judicial by default. Contractual rescission clauses are upheld but court must verify breach. Notice (إعذار) to debtor is generally required before judicial action.

Non-performance by one party must be material and attributable to them.
Notice (إعذار) to debtor before judicial rescission (unless waived or clause dispenses with it).

Restitution of prior performances.

Contractor's minor deviation from technical specs: court likely denies rescission, orders correction.

title: exception of non-performance — دفع عدم التنفيذ
content: Al-Sanhouri treats this as flowing directly from the interdependence of obligations in synallagmatic contracts. It is distinct from rescission: it suspends but does not terminate. The invoking party must themselves have no breach and must be ready to perform. If one party's breach is partial, only the proportional equivalent may be withheld. Courts have equitable discretion to deny the exception if the breach is trivial relative to the suspended performance.

Other party has not performed or offered to perform.
Invoking party is ready and able to perform their own obligation.

title: contractual liability — المسؤولية العقدية
content: Al-Sanhouri's elaboration of the obligation of means vs. result distinction is foundational in Egyptian law. In obligations of means (e.g., doctor's duty to treat), the debtor discharges by exercising due professional care — failure to cure is not breach. In obligations of result (e.g., carrier's obligation to deliver), non-achievement constitutes breach without need to prove fault. The degree of care required in obligations of means (ordinary care, professional care, care of a bonus pater familias) is scaled to contract content. Notice of default (إعذار) is a procedural prerequisite for most damage claims.

sanhouri_position.short: Contractual liability turns on the type of obligation. Obligation of means: debtor shows due care = no liability. Obligation of result: non-achievement = liability unless force majeure. The distinction is fundamental to medical, transport, and professional contracts.

title: tort liability — personal fault (المسؤولية عن الأعمال الشخصية)
content: Al-Sanhouri adopts the objective fault standard. Fault is assessed against what a reasonable person in the same circumstances should have done — not what this particular person intended or was capable of. He distinguishes intentional fault (العمد), gross fault (خطأ جسيم), and ordinary negligence, noting Egyptian tort law does not require a specific degree except in special regimes. Fault requires free volitional act or omission; involuntary reflexes are not fault. Article 163 is a residual general clause covering all non-contractual harm — Egypt's equivalent of the French Article 1382.

title: compensable damage — الضرر الموجب للتعويض
content: Al-Sanhouri insists on certainty: speculative damage does not ground compensation. Future damage is compensable where it inevitably will occur (e.g., permanent disability). He accepts loss of chance as partial compensation — the value of the lost probability, not the full expected outcome. Moral damage (pain, grief, injury to reputation, honor) is explicitly compensable, distinguishing Egyptian law from prior restrictive French approaches. Court has broad equitable discretion in assessing moral damage quantum.

core_principles: Compensable damage must be certain (لا تعويض عن ضرر احتمالي), direct, and caused by defendant's fault.

Future damage is compensable if certain to occur.
Loss of chance is compensable proportionally to the probability of the lost opportunity.

sanhouri_position.short: Damage must be certain and direct. Moral damage is fully compensable. Future certain damage is compensable. Loss of chance is partial compensation proportional to the probability of the lost chance.

Damage must affect a legitimate personal interest of plaintiff.

title: compensation assessment — تقدير التعويض
content: Al-Sanhouri explains that Egyptian tort compensation follows the full-compensation (التعويض الكامل) principle. Court is not bound by amounts claimed; it assesses actual loss. Assessment at judgment date accounts for currency change and evolving damage. Penalty clauses in contracts are binding as agreed damages but under Article 224 the court may reduce if manifestly disproportionate to actual damage or increase if damage exceeded the clause. In joint tortfeasors, each is solidarily liable for the full amount; contribution among them follows fault proportion.

title: vicarious liability — مسؤولية المتبوع عن التابع
content: Al-Sanhouri argues that the presumption of fault in supervising/selecting is practically irrebuttable. The decisive condition is the employment relationship with actual authority and control — not merely contractual employment. The scope of employment condition — act committed 'by reason of or during employment' — is interpreted broadly: if employment provided the occasion or means for the tort, it suffices. Employee need not have acted in employer's interest; only that the job facilitated the act.

title: liability of supervisor — مسؤولية متولي الرقابة
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes supervisor liability from vicarious liability. Supervisor's presumption is rebuttable — unlike the practically irrebuttable employer presumption. The supervisor must show either: (a) they fulfilled their duty of supervision; or (b) the harm was unavoidable even with proper supervision. For schools and institutions, the obligation runs from when the child is under their supervision until released. He notes that obligation to supervise must exist (from law or contract) — mere moral duty to supervise does not suffice.

title: liability for things and animals — المسؤولية عن الأشياء والحيوانات
content: Al-Sanhouri analyzes the custodian as the person with actual direction and control — which may differ from the legal owner. For ordinary things, presumption of fault in custody is rebuttable. For motorized machines (Art. 178), the custodian must show the event was completely beyond their control. He discusses transfer of custody: when hiring out a machine, custody transfers to the hirer if the hirer exercises actual control. Animal owner's liability requires that they were custodians at the relevant time.

title: liability for building collapse — مسؤولية حارس البناء
content: Al-Sanhouri treats Article 177 as establishing a presumption of fault in maintenance (not strict liability). The victim need only show collapse and harm. The custodian must prove: (a) collapse was not due to neglect of maintenance, and (b) there was no pre-existing defect. He distinguishes the building custodian from the things custodian under Article 178 — building liability is specifically fault-presumed, while mechanical things liability approaches strict. The custodian of the building need not be the owner; whoever has actual control and direction bears liability.

exceptions: Proof that collapse was due to act of victim: liability reduced.
Proof that collapse was due to unforeseeable force majeure: liability eliminated.
Proof that there was no neglect in maintenance and no pre-existing defect: liability eliminated.
effects: Custodian fully liable for damage caused by collapse.
Custodian may seek recourse against contractor or maintenance company for their fault.
Solidarity between building owner and custodian if both contributed.
common_disputes: Who is the custodian when property is rented, occupied by tenant, or under construction.
Whether defect was pre-existing or occurred during the custodian's period.
Contractor's independent liability versus building custodian's liability.
practical_examples: Old balcony railing collapses injuring pedestrian below: building custodian presumed liable.
Building under construction collapses: contractor and building owner may both be liable.

title: force majeure and impossibility — القوة القاهرة والاستحالة
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes force majeure from hardship: force majeure makes performance absolutely impossible; hardship makes it excessively burdensome. Three elements must all be present and cumulative. The event must be objectively unforeseeable at contracting. The debtor already in default (إعذار delivered, time passed) cannot invoke subsequent force majeure unless the same damage would have occurred even with timely performance. Economic impossibility is generally insufficient; physical and legal impossibility suffice.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: force majeure and impossibility — القوة القاهرة والاستحالة
core_principles: Force majeure requires three cumulative elements: external event, irresistible, unforeseeable.
Force majeure extinguishes obligation and releases debtor from liability.
Supervening impossibility after default: debtor remains liable even for force majeure events.
Partial impossibility: obligation extinguished as to impossible part; subsists for the rest.

sanhouri_position.short: Force majeure makes performance impossible (distinguished from hardship which makes it excessively burdensome). All three elements must coexist. Debtor in default cannot invoke subsequent force majeure. Economic difficulty alone does not constitute impossibility.

Irresistible: impossible to prevent or overcome.
Unforeseeable at time of contracting.
Makes performance objectively impossible — not merely difficult or expensive.
exceptions: Debtor in default (مدين مماطل) cannot invoke force majeure occurring after default.
Parties may contractually expand or restrict force majeure scope.
Economic hardship alone does not reach the threshold of force majeure.

Counter-obligation in synallagmatic contract also extinguished.
Risk of thing passes: seller bears if possession not yet transferred to buyer.

Currency inconvertibility — force majeure or economic hardship only?
Government regulatory change preventing performance — force majeure or legal impossibility?
practical_examples: Factory destroyed by flood before delivery: force majeure — seller not liable.
Import ban enacted after contract formation preventing contracted delivery: legal impossibility = force majeure.

title: unjust enrichment — الإثراء بلا سبب
content: Al-Sanhouri treats unjust enrichment as a distinct source of obligation, reinforced by Islamic prohibition on unjust acquisition. The action de in rem verso is expressly subsidiary: it cannot circumvent prescription of contract or tort claims. Recovery is limited to the lesser of enrichment or impoverishment — unlike tort which allows full compensation. Good faith of the enriched party is critical: a good-faith enrichee who has consumed the enrichment is not liable for what is no longer 'remaining.'

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Unjust enrichment obliges the enriched party to compensate the impoverished party up to the lesser of enrichment or impoverishment.
Requires: enrichment, corresponding impoverishment, causal link, no legal justification.
Subsidiarity: action unavailable if another legal remedy exists (دعوى احتياطية).
Good faith enrichee who consumed the enrichment without knowledge: limited to current enrichment.

sanhouri_position.short: Unjust enrichment is a residual autonomous source of obligation. Recovery is the lesser of enrichment or impoverishment. Strictly subsidiary — cannot circumvent prescription of contract or tort claims. Good faith enrichee limited to remaining enrichment.

conditions: Enrichment of defendant at plaintiff's expense.
Corresponding impoverishment of plaintiff.
Causal connection between enrichment and impoverishment.
No legal justification (contract, law, or judicial decision).
No other legal action available to plaintiff (strict subsidiarity).
exceptions: Voluntary impoverishment with knowledge of lack of obligation: claim excluded.
Enrichment with legal justification: not unjust.
Good-faith enrichee who consumed enrichment before claim: limited liability.
effects: Obligation to pay the lesser of enrichment or impoverishment.
No punitive element — not a tort remedy.
Bad faith enrichee: full impoverishment + fruits + damages.

Calculating 'remaining enrichment' at time of lawsuit.
Improvements to another's property — unjust enrichment vs. right of removal.
practical_examples: Party mistakenly improves another's land: unjust enrichment claim for cost up to value added.
Prescription bars contract claim: unjust enrichment claim also barred if based on same transaction.

title: undue payment — دفع غير المستحق
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes undue payment as a specific quasi-contract from the general unjust enrichment doctrine. Three scenarios: (1) payment of non-existent debt — always recoverable unless payer knew; (2) payment of another's debt under mistake; (3) payment of condition-dependent debt before condition materialized. Payment of a natural obligation (time-barred debt, moral duty) is valid and irrecoverable — this is the critical rule distinguishing natural from civil obligations.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Payment of what is not owed creates obligation on recipient to return it.
Payer must prove: obligation did not exist (or was extinguished), and payment made in ignorance.
Good faith recipient who consumed the payment: limited restitution obligation (current enrichment only).
Payment of prescribed debt (natural obligation): no recovery — voluntary payment of natural obligation is final.

sanhouri_position.short: Recovery of undue payment requires proof of non-existence of debt and payer's ignorance. Good faith recipient who consumed payment not required to restore more than remaining enrichment. Payment of natural obligation is irrecoverable — this is a critical rule.

conditions: Payment was made.
Payment was not owed: no obligation existed or was already extinguished.
Payer acted in ignorance — believed debt existed.
Good/bad faith of recipient affects extent of recovery obligation.
exceptions: Payment of natural obligation: irrecoverable.
Payment knowing debt did not exist: donation intent presumed — no recovery.
Recipient in good faith who consumed payment: not required to restore beyond current enrichment.
effects: Right to recover the payment amount.
Good faith recipient returns only remaining enrichment.
Bad faith recipient returns principal + fruits + damages.
common_disputes: Proving payer's ignorance of the non-existence of the debt.
Bank overpayment — recovery from recipient who spent the funds.
Recovery from minor who received undue payment.
practical_examples: Employee paid double salary by employer error: employer may recover overpayment.
Debtor repays prescribed debt: valid payment, irrecoverable — natural obligation rule.

title: negotiorum gestio / agency without mandate — الفضالة
content: Al-Sanhouri treats فضالة as a source of obligation distinct from contract and quasi-contract. He requires three conditions: absence of prohibition, absence of authorization, and gestor's intent to benefit the owner (not themselves). The obligation of the owner is conditioned on the usefulness of the intervention — not mere good intention. Gestor must complete the task once begun to avoid greater harm. He distinguishes Egyptian law's 'useful management' requirement from French law's 'necessary management' — broader scope in Egyptian law.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: negotiorum gestio / agency without mandate — الفضالة
core_principles: Negotiorum gestio (فضالة) occurs when a person voluntarily manages another's affairs without authority or prohibition, with intent to benefit the owner.
Gestor must act with care of a reasonable person and complete the task.
Owner (رب العمل) must reimburse necessary and useful expenses if intervention was warranted.
Owner's obligation is conditioned on the usefulness of the intervention, not mere good intent.

sanhouri_position.short: Negotiorum gestio creates mutual obligations. Gestor must manage prudently and complete the task. Owner must reimburse necessary/useful expenses. The decisive condition: owner could not manage themselves and gestor acted in owner's genuine interest.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri treats فضالة as a source of obligation distinct from contract and quasi-contract. conditions: Voluntary intervention without mandate or authorization.
No prohibition by owner (express or reasonably implied).
Gestor's subjective intent to manage owner's affairs, not their own.
Owner was unable to manage themselves at that time (necessity element).
exceptions: Gestor manages in own interest: فضالة does not apply; unjust enrichment may.
Authorized agent: agency rules apply, not فضالة.
Prohibited intervention: owner not obliged to reimburse.
effects: Gestor: must complete management, render account, transfer what acquired on owner's behalf.
Owner: reimburse necessary/useful expenses + obligations contracted by gestor on their behalf.
Gestor not entitled to compensation for time/effort — expense reimbursement only.
common_disputes: Whether gestor acted in owner's or own interest.
Extent of 'useful' expenses reimbursable.
Whether owner's subsequent ratification converts فضالة into mandate — and effects thereof.
practical_examples: Neighbor repairing storm-damaged roof of absent owner: فضالة — owner must reimburse costs.
Person paying another's overdue utility bill to prevent disconnection: possible فضالة.

title: limitation periods — التقادم المسقط
content: Al-Sanhouri's treatment of التقادم المسقط distinguishes it from acquisitive prescription (تقادم مكسب). Prescription extinguishes the civil right to sue but the natural obligation persists — voluntary payment of prescribed debt is irrecoverable. The general 15-year period applies unless a special period is prescribed. Key short periods: 3 years for annulment of voidable contracts; 3 years for tort claims; shorter periods for specific commercial obligations. Interruption (by acknowledgment, lawsuit, or service of legal process) resets the entire period. Suspension (between spouses, guardian and ward, during minority) merely freezes running.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: General prescription period: 15 years for personal civil actions.
Short prescription periods for specific obligations: 3 years (tort), 3 years (annulment), 1 year (commercial short-period obligations).
Prescription extinguishes the right of action — the underlying obligation becomes a natural obligation.
Prescription must be raised by defendant — court cannot apply it ex officio.

sanhouri_position.short: Prescription extinguishes the civil right to sue; the natural obligation persists. Must be pleaded by defendant. Interruption resets the full period. Suspension freezes it during the qualifying event. Voluntary payment of prescribed debt is valid and irrecoverable.

conditions: Passage of prescribed time period without interruption.
Right must have been exercisable throughout (suspension prevented running during qualifying events).
Prescription must be raised as a defense by the party benefiting from it.
exceptions: Prescription does not run between spouses, guardian and ward, or during minority of creditor (suspension).
Acknowledgment of debt by debtor interrupts and resets prescription.
Filing a lawsuit interrupts prescription.
State treasury (قطاع الدولة) — special prescription rules may apply.
effects: Extinguishes right to sue; underlying obligation becomes natural.
Court cannot raise prescription ex officio.
Heir of debtor may waive the prescription benefit.

Whether partial payment interrupts prescription on the whole debt.
Applicable special prescription period for a specific claim.

Contract annulment for fraud: 3 years from discovery of the fraud.

title: law as source of obligation — الالتزام القانوني
content: Al-Sanhouri treats the legal obligation as distinct from the other four sources. He notes that every obligation ultimately traces to the law (which recognizes contract, tort, etc.), but this category refers to obligations directly imposed by a statutory provision without any act or will of the parties. Key examples: obligation of maintenance between family members; guardian's obligations toward ward; good-neighbor obligations. He argues this category is necessary to complete the Code's taxonomy but must be confined to clear statutory impositions.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: law as source of obligation — الالتزام القانوني
core_principles: Law itself is a direct source of obligations independent of any act of will.
Examples: family maintenance (نفقة), guardian's duty of care, good-neighbor relations obligations.
Legal obligations require specific statutory basis — no general clause creates unbounded obligations.
Article 198 recognizes legal obligations as the fifth independent source of obligation.

sanhouri_position.short: Al-Sanhouri takes a restrictive position: unilateral will creates legal obligations only where specifically enacted. He limits the category to clear statutory impositions and warns against over-expansion through broad interpretation.

conditions: Clear statutory provision imposing the obligation.
Existence of the legal relationship from which the obligation arises (kinship, guardianship, etc.).
exceptions: Contractual modification of legally imposed obligations is possible where the law permits.
Public law obligations (taxes, regulatory duties) are not civil legal obligations in this sense.
effects: Obligation is binding regardless of party consent.
Enforceable through general compulsory execution rules.
Breach of legal obligation may simultaneously constitute tort fault under Article 163.
common_disputes: Scope of maintenance obligations among extended family.
Whether specific professional duties are legal obligations or mere standards of care.
practical_examples: Father's obligation to support minor children: legal obligation — arises from law, not contract.
Neighbor's obligation not to excavate in a way endangering adjacent building: legal obligation.

title: unilateral will as source of obligation — الإرادة المنفردة
content: Al-Sanhouri engages with the German-French debate and rejects the German theory (which makes unilateral declaration broadly binding). Only specific Code cases create binding unilateral obligations. The primary case is the public promise of reward (Art. 162): a person publicly promising a reward for performing an act is bound to pay it to the performer. Promisor may revoke before performance through equivalent publicity. Whether performer must have known of the promise before performing is disputed — Egyptian courts are divided.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: unilateral will as source of obligation — الإرادة المنفردة
core_principles: Egyptian Civil Code recognizes unilateral will as a limited independent source of obligation.
Public promise of reward: binding on promisor even before acceptance if specified act is performed.
Promisor may revoke before performance, but revocation must use equivalent public channel.
Al-Sanhouri rejects the broad German theory of unilateral will as a general source.

sanhouri_position.short: Al-Sanhouri is restrictive: unilateral will creates obligation only in specific statutory cases. The primary case is the public reward promise (Art. 162). The broad German theory is rejected; Islamic law influence supports limiting unilateral binding declarations.

conditions: For public promise of reward: promise must be public, addressed to unidentified persons.
Act specified in the promise must be performed.
Promise must have been in effect and not revoked at time of performance.
exceptions: Revocation of promise before performance: effective if revoked through equivalent public channel.
Private unilateral promise: generally not binding absent statutory basis or acceptance.
effects: Promisor bound to pay reward to first performer.
If multiple persons perform simultaneously: reward shared equally.
Promisor cannot add conditions after performance.

What constitutes 'equivalent publicity' for revocation.
Competing performers — who performed 'first' and whether simultaneous performance requires sharing.

Architect publicly promising free design for charity: not binding as unilateral will absent acceptance.

title: abuse of rights — التعسف في استعمال الحق
content: Al-Sanhouri treats Article 5 as one of the Egyptian Code's most innovative provisions, drawing explicitly from Islamic jurisprudence (hadith: 'no harm and no reciprocal harm') and the social function theory of rights. Three alternative tests for abuse: (1) malicious intent with no benefit to oneself; (2) potential harm grossly exceeds benefit; (3) benefit sought is illegitimate or non-serious. These are alternatives, not cumulative. He emphasizes this applies in property law (use of land), procedural law (vexatious litigation), and contract law.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: abuse of rights — التعسف في استعمال الحق
core_principles: Exercise of a right becomes unlawful if: (1) sole purpose is to harm another; or (2) harm grossly disproportionate to benefit; or (3) benefit sought is illegitimate.
Any one of three criteria is sufficient — they are alternative, not cumulative.
Abuse of rights is treated as a tort — creates liability as if an unlawful act.
Remedies: injunction, damages, or dismantlement of abusive work.

sanhouri_position.short: Article 5 adopts a multi-criterion theory of abuse of rights. All three criteria reflect Islamic jurisprudence (لا ضرر ولا ضرار) and the social function theory of rights (Duguit). Any single criterion suffices. One of Al-Sanhouri's most celebrated innovations in the Egyptian Code.

conditions: Exercise of a formally recognized legal right.
Exercise meets at least one criterion: malicious intent, gross disproportion of harm to benefit, or illegitimate purpose.
Actual or threatened harm to another.
exceptions: Right exercised for genuine legitimate interest: no abuse even if harm to neighbor results.
Normal commercial competition causing harm to competitors: no abuse unless malicious.
effects: Court may enjoin abusive exercise of right.
Damages for harm caused by abusive exercise.
Court may order dismantlement of work constituting an abuse.
common_disputes: Digging well to divert neighbor's water supply with no benefit to oneself: abuse.
Vexatious litigation (مماطلة قضائية): abuse of procedural right to litigate.
Industrial fence built solely to block competitor's view: abuse.
practical_examples: Owner building high wall solely to block neighbor's light with no benefit to themselves: abuse of property right.
Filing meritless lawsuits sequentially to damage competitor: abuse of right to litigate.

title: extinction of obligation — payment and performance (الوفاء)
content: Al-Sanhouri systematizes the law of payment as the primary mode of obligation extinction. Payment must be of the exact object owed, to the person entitled to receive, by the person capable of paying. Partial payment: creditor cannot be forced to accept unless court grants debtor a grace period. Third-party payment: creditor must generally accept unless the obligation was stipulated as personal (intuitu personae). Subrogation rights of third-party payer depend on debtor's consent to payment.

source_fields.topic: extinction of obligation — payment and performance (الوفاء)
core_principles: Payment (الوفاء) is the primary mode of extinguishing obligations — debtor performs what was owed.
Payment must be complete: creditor cannot be forced to accept partial payment.
Third party may pay on debtor's behalf — creditor must accept unless personal performance was stipulated.
Payment by third party without debtor's knowledge or against debtor's will: limited recourse rights.

sanhouri_position.short: Wafaa (وفاء) extinguishes obligation upon complete performance. Third-party payment is valid; creditor must accept. Third party who pays with debtor's knowledge is subrogated to creditor's rights. Payment against debtor's will: limited to unjust enrichment recovery.

conditions: Payment of exact subject matter owed (genus, quality, quantity).
Payment to the creditor or authorized representative.
Payment by person with capacity to alienate (if payment involves transfer of ownership).
Complete payment — no obligation to accept partial performance.
exceptions: Court may grant debtor a grace period (مهلة قضائية) allowing deferred payment.
Creditor who wrongfully refuses payment: debtor may make formal tender (عرض حقيقي) and deposit.
Payment to apparent creditor in good faith is valid against true creditor.
effects: Obligation extinguished upon complete payment.
All accessory obligations (guarantees, mortgages) extinguished simultaneously.
Third-party payer acquires subrogation rights depending on circumstances of payment.

Payment to apparent creditor — protection of good faith payer.
Whether performance meets exact specification in obligations of specific thing.
practical_examples: Debtor tenders exact amount owed; creditor refuses: debtor deposits with court — obligation extinguished.
Third party pays debtor's debt with debtor's knowledge: subrogated to creditor's rights including guarantees.

title: set-off — المقاصة
content: Al-Sanhouri analyzes set-off as automatic (مقاصة قانونية) once the three conditions (certainty, maturity, liquidity/fungibility) are simultaneously met — though parties must invoke it before the court to produce procedural effect. He stresses the retroactive effect: set-off extinguishes from the moment conditions were met, not from invocation. This has important consequences for interest and guarantees that attached between those two moments. He distinguishes legal set-off from agreed set-off (مقاصة اتفاقية) and judicial set-off (مقاصة قضائية).

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Set-off (مقاصة) extinguishes two mutual obligations up to the amount of the lesser.
Legal set-off operates automatically when: both debts are certain, due, and liquid (fungible same kind).
Set-off does not operate against obligations to return stolen property, harm-causing deposits, or maintenance obligations.
Judicial set-off requires court declaration where debt is not yet certain or liquid.

sanhouri_position.short: Legal set-off operates automatically when conditions are met — no need for party invocation. It extinguishes both debts from the moment conditions were satisfied, retroactively affecting any intervening security interests.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri analyzes set-off as automatic (مقاصة قانونية) once the three conditions (certainty, maturity, liquidity/fungibility) are simultaneously met — though parties must invoke it before the court to produce procedural effect. He distinguishes legal set-off from agreed set-off (مقاصة اتفاقية) and judicial set-off (مقاصة قضائية).

conditions: Both debts owed between the same two parties in the same capacity.
Both debts are of the same kind (fungible — usually money).
Both debts are certain (محقق الوجود), mature (حال الأداء), and liquid (معين المقدار).
exceptions: No set-off against obligation to return stolen or lost property.
No set-off against obligation arising from harmful deposit.
No set-off against maintenance (نفقة) obligations.
No set-off if one debt arose from tortious act the law prohibits set-off for.
effects: Both obligations extinguished up to the amount of the lesser debt.
Retroactive extinction from moment conditions were met.
Accessory obligations (guarantees, mortgages) on the extinguished portions also extinguished.
common_disputes: Whether a debt is sufficiently 'liquid' (محدد المقدار) for legal set-off.
Set-off in bankruptcy — whether debts arising before insolvency may be set off.
Set-off against assigned debt — debtor's set-off rights against the assignee.
practical_examples: A owes B EGP 100,000; B owes A EGP 70,000 — both mature: automatic set-off of EGP 70,000.
Debtor attempts set-off against maintenance payment: prohibited.

title: novation — التجديد
content: Al-Sanhouri treats novation as a mode of extinction of obligations by substitution. Three types: (1) substitution of new object (تجديد بتغيير المحل); (2) substitution of debtor (انقلاب الدين / expromissio); (3) substitution of creditor (تجديد بتغيير الدائن). Intent to novate is critical and must be clear — it is never presumed. The extinction of accessory obligations (guarantees, pledges) is a major practical consequence: guarantors are released upon novation unless they expressly consent to remain bound under the new obligation.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Novation (تجديد) extinguishes an existing obligation by creating a new one in its place.
Novation requires: existing obligation, new obligation, change in essential element, and intent to novate.
Intent to novate (نية التجديد) is not presumed — must be explicit or unmistakably clear.
Novation extinguishes accessory obligations (guarantees, mortgages) on the old obligation.

sanhouri_position.short: Novation requires clear intent and an essential change. Intent is not presumed; doubt favors continuation of old obligation. Novation extinguishes the old obligation with all its accessories — a critical practical consequence for secured creditors.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri treats novation as a mode of extinction of obligations by substitution. Three types: (1) substitution of new object (تجديد بتغيير المحل); (2) substitution of debtor (انقلاب الدين / expromissio); (3) substitution of creditor (تجديد بتغيير الدائن). Intent to novate is critical and must be clear — it is never presumed. The extinction of accessory obligations (guarantees, pledges) is a major practical consequence: guarantors are released upon novation unless they expressly consent to remain bound under the new obligation.

conditions: Existing valid obligation (void obligation cannot be novated).
New valid obligation to replace it.
Essential change: in subject matter, debtor, or creditor.
Clear intent to novate (نية التجديد) — not presumed.
exceptions: Mere modification of payment terms or modalities is not novation.
Guarantor's liability survives novation only if they expressly consented to remain bound.
Defective obligation can sometimes be novated if parties intended to cure the defect.
effects: Old obligation extinguished with all its accessories.
New obligation arises with fresh prescription period.
Guarantors, pledges, and mortgages on old obligation are released unless they consented.
common_disputes: Whether a debt restructuring agreement constitutes novation (with accessory extinction) or mere modification.
Whether guarantor's liability survives when principal obligation is novated.
Whether debt acknowledgment in new instrument is novation or mere evidence.
practical_examples: Debtor's personal obligation converted into obligation of a new company: novation by change of debtor.
Old mortgage-secured debt restructured in new agreement: novation or modification — critical for guarantor.

title: assignment of debt — حوالة الحق
content: Al-Sanhouri treats حوالة الحق as a mode of transferring obligations. The debtor need not consent — they are a third party to the assignment. Protection: debtor cannot be prejudiced; they retain all defenses against the assignee that they had against the assignor at time of notification. Priority between competing assignees of the same debt: first to notify the debtor prevails. Assignor is liable for existence and enforceability of the right assigned — but not for the debtor's solvency unless specifically warranted.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Assignor (creditor) may transfer his right to a third party (assignee) without debtor's consent.
Assignment is effective against debtor only after notification or acceptance.
Debtor may raise against assignee all defenses available against assignor at time of notification.
Assignor warrants existence and current enforceability of the assigned right — not debtor's solvency (unless warranted).

sanhouri_position.short: Assignment of credit transfers the right without debtor's consent. Debtor is protected by requirement of notification before assignment binds him. Assignor warrants existence of right. Priority between competing assignees: first to notify the debtor prevails.

Right assigned must be transferable (not strictly personal obligations).
Notification to debtor (or debtor's acceptance) for assignment to be effective against debtor.
For priority: first notification to debtor prevails.
exceptions: Rights strictly personal to the creditor cannot be assigned (e.g., right to maintenance).
Contractual prohibition of assignment is effective against assignee with notice.
Assignment of future rights possible but subject to conditions on existence.

Debtor's defenses against assignor survive and can be raised against assignee.
Assignor warrants existence and enforceability — liable if right was non-existent or extinguished.

Assignor's warranty of solvency — express vs. implied.
Priority between multiple assignees of the same right.
practical_examples: Bank assigns mortgage loan receivable to securitization fund: valid without borrower's consent.
Debtor had set-off right against assignor at notification date: can raise against assignee.

title: personal guarantee — الكفالة الشخصية
content: Al-Sanhouri treats guarantee as a strictly accessory obligation: the guarantor's liability cannot exceed the principal obligation in amount or burdenousness. All defenses of the principal debtor (except those personal to the debtor, like prescription of the debtor's personal action) may be raised by the guarantor. Benefit of discussion (حق التجريد) requires the creditor to first proceed against the debtor's assets. Co-guarantors have benefit of division (حق التقسيم). Both benefits may be waived — and usually are in commercial/banking practice through joint guarantee clauses.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Guarantee (كفالة) is a personal accessory obligation: guarantor binds themselves to creditor for performance of debtor's obligation.
Guarantee is accessory — its validity depends on validity of guaranteed obligation.
Guarantor has benefit of discussion (حق التجريد): creditor must first exhaust debtor's assets.
Joint guarantee (كفالة تضامنية) waives benefit of discussion; guarantor liable simultaneously with debtor.

sanhouri_position.short: Guarantee is strictly accessory — follows the principal obligation. Guarantor benefits from all defenses of the principal debtor. Benefit of discussion must be expressly invoked. Joint guarantee eliminates this benefit and is the commercial standard.

conditions: Valid principal obligation to guarantee.
Guarantee agreement — need not be in same form as principal obligation (generally).
Guarantor has legal capacity and is not under incapacity.
Guarantee is not subject to condition that defeats its accessory nature.
exceptions: Void principal obligation: guarantee is void.
Guarantor may not guarantee more than the principal obligation.
Express waiver of benefit of discussion: guarantor liable alongside debtor.

Guarantor subrogated to creditor's rights against debtor upon payment.
Guarantor's obligation extinguished when principal obligation is extinguished.

Guarantor's liability when principal obligation is partially extinguished by set-off or partial payment.
Whether novation of principal obligation releases guarantor who did not consent.
practical_examples: Bank loan with personal guarantor: standard practice; guarantor typically waives benefit of discussion.
Novation of guaranteed debt: guarantor released unless they expressly consented to new obligation.

title: simulation — الصورية
content: Al-Sanhouri systematizes simulation by distinguishing absolute simulation (العقد الصوري المطلق — where there is no real agreement at all) from relative simulation (العقد الصوري النسبي — where a real different agreement underlies the apparent one). In absolute simulation, the contract is void between parties and against all. In relative simulation, the hidden contract is valid between parties if it meets all legal conditions. Third-party good-faith reliance on the apparent contract is protected — a key principle protecting commercial security. He stresses simulation is neutral until it causes harm.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Simulation (الصورية) is the gap between the apparent contract (العقد الظاهر) and the hidden real agreement (العقد المستتر).
Between parties: the hidden real contract governs, not the apparent one.
Against third parties acting in good faith relying on apparent contract: the apparent contract prevails.
Creditors and heirs may challenge simulation (دعوى الصورية) to apply the hidden contract.

sanhouri_position.short: The hidden contract governs between parties. Third parties in good faith are protected by the apparent contract. Simulation is not inherently illegal — it becomes so only when used to defraud creditors or circumvent legal prohibition.
