conditions: Apparent contract: externally visible agreement differing from true intent.
Hidden contract (counter-letter — ورقة الضد): the real agreement between parties.
Parties must have intended the gap between apparent and hidden.
exceptions: If hidden contract is itself unlawful: void as to both parties.
Good faith third parties relying on apparent contract are fully protected.
Creditors (دائنون) may invoke the hidden contract against the simulation.
effects: Between parties: hidden contract governs.
Against good faith third parties: apparent contract governs.
Simulation designed to defraud creditors: creditors may invoke the hidden (true) contract.
common_disputes: Whether a transaction is simulated sale or true alienation (anti-creditor fraud).
Hidden usurious interest rate concealed under apparent commission arrangement.
Simulated donation concealing true sale price to evade taxes.
practical_examples: Apparent sale at EGP 1M with hidden agreement that seller retains possession: relative simulation.
Apparent donation between spouses to hide true consideration: simulation.

title: pre-contractual liability — المسؤولية قبل التعاقدية (culpa in contrahendo)
content: Al-Sanhouri discusses culpa in contrahendo following Ihering's doctrine. In Egyptian law, pre-contractual liability is grounded in the general tort provision (Art. 163) rather than in an independent doctrine. The critical element is bad faith: conducting negotiations while knowing no contract would result, thereby inducing the other party to waste resources. Compensation is limited to negative interest (المصلحة السلبية): actual reliance expenses and foregone alternative opportunities — not the profit that would have been made under the prospective contract (positive interest). He notes this area was not codified separately, leaving courts to apply tort principles.

Compensation limited to negative interest (المصلحة السلبية): expenses incurred + lost opportunities foregone.
Mere breaking off of negotiations is not itself unlawful — bad faith is the decisive element.

Party broke off negotiations in bad faith — knowing no contract would result.
Other party relied on negotiations and incurred expenses or foregone other opportunities.
Causal link between bad faith rupture and the reliance damage.
exceptions: Breaking off negotiations for legitimate reason (better offer, changed circumstances): lawful.

Calculating foregone alternative opportunities.
Whether preliminary agreement (heads of terms) creates contractual pre-contractual duty.
practical_examples: Party negotiates purchase of business for months, inducing other to turn away buyers, then withdraws without reason: bad faith.
Developer negotiates construction contract, contractor commissions architect's drawings, developer withdraws: pre-contractual liability.

title: alternative and facultative obligations — الالتزام البديل والاختياري
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes alternative obligations (where the object is one of several, all constituting the obligation) from facultative obligations (where a single object is owed but substitution is permitted as a faculty). The distinction matters when one performance becomes impossible: in alternative obligations, the remaining performance is owed; in facultative obligations, if the primary performance becomes impossible through no fault of debtor, the whole obligation is extinguished. Default holder of choice is the debtor. If creditor holds choice and primary performance perishes through debtor's fault, creditor may demand the other or damages.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: alternative and facultative obligations — الالتزام البديل والاختياري
core_principles: Alternative obligation: debtor owes one of two or more performances; choosing which one generally belongs to the debtor.
Once debtor makes the choice and creditor is notified, the obligation becomes simple.
Facultative obligation: debtor owes one defined performance but has the faculty to discharge by substituting another.
If the chosen performance becomes impossible, in alternative obligations the other performance becomes due.

sanhouri_position.short: In alternative obligations, choice belongs to debtor unless expressly given to creditor. Once chosen, the obligation concentrates. If one performance perishes through debtor's fault, creditor may claim the other or damages.

Choice must be exercised clearly and communicated.
For facultative: contract specifies one primary performance with right of substitution.
exceptions: If all alternative performances become impossible through force majeure: obligation extinguished.
If one performance becomes impossible through debtor's fault and creditor holds choice: creditor may claim remaining or damages.

Accessories (guarantees, pledges) attach to chosen performance from time of obligation.
For facultative: substitution discharges the original obligation fully.
common_disputes: Whether the contractual language creates an alternative or facultative obligation.
Who holds the right of election when contract is silent.
Effect of partial impossibility on alternative obligations.
practical_examples: Contractor may deliver either product A or product B: alternative obligation — debtor chooses.
Sale of specific car with option to substitute a different model: facultative obligation.

title: joint and several obligations — التضامن
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes passive solidarity (the commercially important form) from active solidarity (rare in practice). Passive solidarity: creditor has full choice among debtors; partial performance does not release others as to balance. Internal contribution between solidary debtors follows their proportional shares — equally if no agreement. He notes that in commercial law, solidarity is presumed between co-debtors, unlike civil law. Defenses personal to one solidary debtor (prescription, set-off) cannot be used by others; defenses common to all (void obligation) benefit all.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Passive solidarity (تضامن بين المدينين): creditor may demand full performance from any solidary debtor.
Active solidarity (تضامن بين الدائنين): any solidary creditor may demand full performance from debtor.
Solidarity is not presumed — requires agreement, law, or judgment.
Payment by one solidary debtor releases all; creditor's acts binding on all solidary creditors.

sanhouri_position.short: Solidarity is not presumed in civil law; it must be expressly stipulated or imposed by law. In commercial matters, solidarity between co-debtors is presumed. Each solidary debtor is liable for the whole but has contribution rights against co-debtors.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes passive solidarity (the commercially important form) from active solidarity (rare in practice). conditions: Express stipulation in contract, statutory provision, or judicial decision.
In commercial transactions: solidarity presumed between co-debtors.
Full obligation owed by each solidary debtor to creditor.
exceptions: Defense personal to one solidary debtor (e.g., his personal prescription period ran) cannot be used by others.
Common defense (unlawful object) extinguishes obligation for all.
Creditor's act releasing one solidary debtor releases others proportionally for the released share.
effects: Creditor may sue any or all solidary debtors simultaneously or successively.
Full payment by one debtor releases all; creditor cannot recover twice.
Paying debtor has contribution right against co-debtors for their proportional shares.
common_disputes: Whether solidarity exists in a civil co-debtor situation absent express agreement.
Contribution rights when one solidary debtor is insolvent.
Effect of creditor's release of one solidary debtor on others.
practical_examples: Three partners jointly and severally guarantee a loan: creditor may demand full amount from any one.
Two tortfeasors jointly cause damage: solidary liability to victim (by law).

title: obligations with modalities — الأجل والشرط
content: Al-Sanhouri systematizes modalities of obligations. Key distinction: conditions affect obligation's existence (suspensive condition suspends birth; resolutory condition creates obligation subject to extinction). Terms affect only the time of performance, not existence. Conditions have retroactive effect upon occurrence — treated as if obligation always existed from formation. He emphasizes that purely potestative conditions (شرط إرادي محض — dependent solely on debtor's will, e.g., 'if I wish') are void as they make the obligation illusory.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Suspensive condition (شرط واقف): obligation arises only upon occurrence of a future uncertain event.
Resolutory condition (شرط فاسخ): obligation extinguished upon occurrence of a future uncertain event.
Suspensive term (أجل واقف): obligation exists but performance is deferred to a future certain date.
Condition has retroactive effect upon occurrence — term does not.

sanhouri_position.short: Conditions affect the existence of the obligation (suspensive = birth; resolutory = death). Terms affect the enforceability only. Condition's retroactive effect is the key legal consequence. Potestative conditions dependent solely on debtor's will are void.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri systematizes modalities of obligations. Key distinction: conditions affect obligation's existence (suspensive condition suspends birth; resolutory condition creates obligation subject to extinction). Terms affect only the time of performance, not existence. Conditions have retroactive effect upon occurrence — treated as if obligation always existed from formation. He emphasizes that purely potestative conditions (شرط إرادي محض — dependent solely on debtor's will, e.g., 'if I wish') are void as they make the obligation illusory.

conditions: For suspensive condition: event must be future, uncertain, and not purely dependent on debtor's will.
For term: event must be future and certain (even if date unknown, as in death).
Condition must not be impossible, unlawful, or contrary to public order (renders obligation void).
exceptions: Purely potestative condition (dependent solely on debtor's will): void — nullifies the obligation.
Mixed potestative condition (partly dependent on debtor, partly on external events): valid.
Unlawful condition in a donation: voids the donation.
effects: Suspensive condition met: obligation retroactively deemed to have existed from formation.
Resolutory condition met: obligation retroactively extinguished — restitution obligations arise.
Term expires: obligation immediately enforceable; acceleration on insolvency of debtor.
common_disputes: Whether a condition has been fulfilled — especially conditions involving third-party actions.
Whether the debtor's bad faith prevented fulfillment — deemed fulfilled.
Whether a condition is purely potestative and therefore void.
practical_examples: Sale conditional on buyer obtaining bank finance: suspensive condition — obligation born on finance approval.
Donation on condition donor survives 5 years: resolutory condition — obligation extinguished if donor dies within 5 years.

title: legal and conventional subrogation — الحلول
content: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes subrogation (حلول) from assignment of debt (حوالة الحق): subrogation arises from payment and substitutes the payor in the creditor's position with identical rights; assignment is consensual transfer. Key legal subrogation cases: (1) third party paying with legal interest in extinguishing the debt; (2) guarantor paying the principal debt; (3) co-debtor paying more than their share. Subrogation cap: payor cannot recover more than paid. This prevents overcompensation while preserving the accessories essential to recovery.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Subrogation (حلول): a third party who pays a debt steps into the creditor's shoes and acquires all the creditor's rights, accessories, and securities.
Legal subrogation operates automatically in specific cases; conventional subrogation requires agreement.
Subrogation transfers the right as-is — with all its accessories (guarantees, mortgages, privileges).
Subrogated party cannot recover more than they actually paid.

sanhouri_position.short: Subrogation substitutes the paying third party for the original creditor with all accessories. Legal subrogation occurs by operation of law in specified cases (co-debtor paying, guarantor paying). It is distinguished from assignment: subrogation arises from payment, assignment from agreement.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri distinguishes subrogation (حلول) from assignment of debt (حوالة الحق): subrogation arises from payment and substitutes the payor in the creditor's position with identical rights; assignment is consensual transfer. Key legal subrogation cases: (1) third party paying with legal interest in extinguishing the debt; (2) guarantor paying the principal debt; (3) co-debtor paying more than their share. Subrogation cap: payor cannot recover more than paid. This prevents overcompensation while preserving the accessories essential to recovery.

conditions: Payment of the debt by a third party (not the principal debtor).
For legal subrogation: payment by party with legitimate interest (guarantor, co-debtor, real-security provider).
For conventional subrogation: express agreement at time of payment.
exceptions: Subrogee cannot recover more than actually paid.
Debtor's personal defenses against original creditor may still apply against subrogee.
Partial payment creates partial subrogation; original creditor retains priority for unpaid balance.
effects: Subrogee acquires all creditor's rights including guarantees, mortgages, and privileges.
Subrogee can enforce against debtor and any real/personal security providers.
Original creditor is preferred over partial subrogee for the unpaid balance.
common_disputes: Whether payment was made under circumstances triggering legal subrogation.
Priority between partial subrogee and original creditor for remaining balance.
Guarantor's subrogation rights against co-guarantors after paying the whole debt.
practical_examples: Guarantor pays bank loan in full: subrogated to bank's rights including mortgage over debtor's property.
Co-debtor pays full solidary debt: subrogated against co-debtors for their shares.

title: remission of debt — الإبراء
content: Al-Sanhouri analyzes remission as a unilateral legal act (tasarruf iradi infiradi) — not a bilateral contract — because the creditor's unilateral intent suffices to create the legal effect, subject to the debtor's right to refuse. If the debtor refuses, the obligation revives. Remission of the principal debt extinguishes accessory obligations (guarantees, pledges) automatically. Remission may be express or tacit (e.g., voluntary delivery of the debt instrument to the debtor). Remission by the creditor to one solidary debtor releases the others pro rata.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Remission (إبراء) is the creditor's gratuitous release of the debtor from all or part of the obligation.
Remission is a unilateral act — it does not require debtor's acceptance; debtor may reject it.
Remission extinguishes the obligation and all its accessories (guarantees, pledges).
Partial remission is valid and extinguishes the obligation to the extent of the release.

sanhouri_position.short: Remission is a unilateral gratuitous act of the creditor. Debtor may refuse. Upon acceptance (implied or express), obligation extinguished with all accessories. Al-Sanhouri treats it as a unilateral legal act, not a contract.
sanhouri_position.professional: Al-Sanhouri analyzes remission as a unilateral legal act (tasarruf iradi infiradi) — not a bilateral contract — because the creditor's unilateral intent suffices to create the legal effect, subject to the debtor's right to refuse. If the debtor refuses, the obligation revives. Remission of the principal debt extinguishes accessory obligations (guarantees, pledges) automatically. conditions: Creditor must have capacity to dispose of the right gratuitously.
Remission must be definite and clear — doubt interpreted against extinction.
Debtor has right to refuse (especially if remission has conditions attached).
exceptions: Remission to one solidary debtor: releases others only for their proportional share.
Remission cannot harm creditor's own creditors — Paulian action may set aside fraudulent remissions.
Voluntary delivery of debt instrument by creditor to debtor: presumption of remission.
effects: Obligation extinguished with all its accessories.
Solidary co-debtors: released proportionally if remission is to one.
Guarantors: released when principal obligation is remitted.
common_disputes: Whether delivery of document proves remission or merely payment.
Whether remission was conditional and condition has been met.
Partial remission in settlement agreements — scope of release.
practical_examples: Creditor tears up promissory note and returns it to debtor: presumed remission.
Settlement agreement releasing all claims under a contract: express remission.

title: transfer of debt — حوالة الدين
content: Al-Sanhouri treats حوالة الدين as the mirror image of حوالة الحق. The critical difference: debt transfer requires creditor's consent (because the identity of the debtor matters to the creditor), whereas assignment of credit does not require debtor's consent. Upon transfer with creditor's consent and release, original debtor is fully discharged. Personal accessories (personal guarantee by original debtor's guarantor) are extinguished automatically unless the guarantor separately consents to remain bound under the new debtor's obligation.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Transfer of debt (حوالة الدين) substitutes a new debtor for the original debtor — requires creditor's consent.
Creditor consent releases the original debtor; without release, original debtor remains secondarily liable.
New debtor may raise against creditor all defenses that were available to original debtor at time of transfer.
Transfer of debt extinguishes accessories attached to original debtor's personal obligation unless they consent.

sanhouri_position.short: Transfer of debt requires creditor's consent — unlike assignment of credit which needs none. Without creditor's express release of original debtor, both remain liable. Accessories personal to original debtor are extinguished; real security may survive if security-provider consents.

The critical difference: debt transfer requires creditor's consent (because the identity of the debtor matters to the creditor), whereas assignment of credit does not require debtor's consent. Upon transfer with creditor's consent and release, original debtor is fully discharged. Personal accessories (personal guarantee by original debtor's guarantor) are extinguished automatically unless the guarantor separately consents to remain bound under the new debtor's obligation.

conditions: Agreement between original debtor and new debtor (or new debtor and creditor).
Creditor's consent — either to the substitution alone or with release of original debtor.
Without release: original debtor remains a secondary guarantor of new debtor's performance.
exceptions: Without express release: original debtor remains liable if new debtor defaults.
Guarantor of original debt: released unless they consent to guarantee new debtor.
New debtor cannot use defenses personal to original debtor (e.g., original debtor's personal prescription).
effects: With release: original debtor fully discharged; new debtor solely liable.
Without release: original debtor secondarily liable.
Creditor acquires rights against new debtor; personal accessories extinguished.
common_disputes: Whether creditor's consent was given to substitution with or without release of original debtor.
Guarantor's status after debt transfer — consent requirement.
Corporate restructuring — transfer of debts between group companies.
practical_examples: Real estate buyer assumes seller's mortgage with bank's consent: debt transfer.
Company assigns all its liabilities to subsidiary: requires individual creditors' consent.

title: proof of obligations — إثبات الالتزامات
content: Al-Sanhouri examines proof (إثبات) as integral to the law of obligations. The written instrument rule protects against fraud in high-value transactions. Below the threshold (EGP 1,000 in the Civil Code era), oral testimony and all means are admissible. Above the threshold: writing required; oral testimony cannot prove the contract or contradict it. Exceptions: commercial contracts (governed by commercial law), commencement of written proof (مبدأ الثبوت بالكتابة) — a writing that makes the claim plausible reduces the bar for oral testimony. He distinguishes authentic instruments (المحررات الرسمية) from private instruments (المحررات العرفية).

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

core_principles: Claimant bears burden of proving their claim; defendant bears burden of proving their defense.
Contractual obligations above EGP 1,000 must be proved by writing — oral testimony is inadmissible to prove or contradict a written instrument.
Judicial presumptions, confession (إقرار), and oath supplement documentary proof.
Presumptions established by law are binding unless rebutted — some are irrebuttable.

sanhouri_position.short: Al-Sanhouri treats proof as a procedural extension of substantive law. Written proof is mandatory for contracts above the statutory threshold. The threshold distinguishes commercial from civil transactions. Confession is the strongest proof — it is binding on the confessor.

Below the threshold (EGP 1,000 in the Civil Code era), oral testimony and all means are admissible. Above the threshold: writing required; oral testimony cannot prove the contract or contradict it. Exceptions: commercial contracts (governed by commercial law), commencement of written proof (مبدأ الثبوت بالكتابة) — a writing that makes the claim plausible reduces the bar for oral testimony. He distinguishes authentic instruments (المحررات الرسمية) from private instruments (المحررات العرفية).

conditions: Claimant establishes obligation by: authentic instrument, private instrument, admission, testimony (where admissible), judicial presumptions, or oath.
Writing required for contracts above EGP 1,000 in value.
Commercial contracts: all means of proof admissible regardless of value.
exceptions: Commercial transactions: oral testimony always admissible.
Commencement of written proof (مبدأ الثبوت بالكتابة) permits supplementary oral testimony.
Material impossibility of obtaining writing (fire, flood, sudden urgent transaction): oral testimony exceptionally permitted.
effects: Authenticated instrument: full proof unless forgery proved.
Private instrument: full proof between parties as to its contents.
Confession: binding on the confessor — strongest proof.
common_disputes: Whether electronic correspondence constitutes 'writing' for purposes of the threshold.
Whether a document amounts to commencement of written proof.
Admissibility of oral testimony to clarify (not contradict) written instrument.
practical_examples: Oral agreement to buy car for EGP 200,000: cannot be proved by oral testimony — writing required.
WhatsApp exchange confirming contract terms: may qualify as written evidence depending on court.

title: creditor remedies — indirect action and Paulian action (الدعوى غير المباشرة والدعوى البولصية)
content: Al-Sanhouri systematizes the two principal creditor remedies for protecting the general guarantee. The oblique action (دعوى غير المباشرة) allows the creditor to stand in the debtor's shoes and exercise rights the debtor negligently fails to exercise. The Paulian action (دعوى عدم النفاذ / دعوى البولصية) attacks completed fraudulent dispositions: transfers, remissions, or other acts reducing the debtor's assets. For the Paulian action, 'fraud' means knowledge by the debtor that the disposition would harm creditors — not necessarily malicious intent. Gratuitous dispositions: no need to prove donee's knowledge. Onerous dispositions: must also prove the acquirer's knowledge.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: creditor remedies — indirect action and Paulian action (الدعوى غير المباشرة والدعوى البولصية)
core_principles: Indirect (oblique) action: creditor exercises debtor's rights if debtor neglects to do so, to protect the general guarantee.
Paulian action: creditor challenges debtor's fraudulent dispositions that diminish assets at creditors' expense.
For Paulian action: creditor must prove debtor's act caused insolvency or worsened it, and debtor acted with fraud.
Paulian action makes disposition ineffective as against the challenging creditor only — not voided absolutely.

sanhouri_position.short: Creditor's oblique action is defensive — exercising debtor's neglected rights to preserve the general guarantee. Paulian action is aggressive — challenging fraudulent dispositions. Both protect the general guarantee (الضمان العام). Paulian action requires fraud (علم بالضرر), not necessarily intent to harm.

The oblique action (دعوى غير المباشرة) allows the creditor to stand in the debtor's shoes and exercise rights the debtor negligently fails to exercise. The Paulian action (دعوى عدم النفاذ / دعوى البولصية) attacks completed fraudulent dispositions: transfers, remissions, or other acts reducing the debtor's assets. For the Paulian action, 'fraud' means knowledge by the debtor that the disposition would harm creditors — not necessarily malicious intent. Gratuitous dispositions: no need to prove donee's knowledge. Onerous dispositions: must also prove the acquirer's knowledge.

conditions: For oblique action: (1) creditor has valid debt; (2) debtor neglects to exercise a right; (3) neglect harms creditor's security.
For Paulian action: (1) creditor has valid debt prior to disposition; (2) disposition caused or worsened insolvency; (3) debtor knew of harm to creditors; (4) for onerous acts: acquirer also knew.
exceptions: Rights strictly personal to debtor (maintenance, moral rights) cannot be exercised by oblique action.
Paulian action cannot reach acts predating the creditor's claim without special circumstances.
Good faith acquirer for value protected against Paulian action unless they knew of fraud.
effects: Oblique action: recovered assets enter debtor's estate for all creditors' benefit.
Paulian action: disposition rendered ineffective (عدم النفاذ) only as to the challenging creditor.
Other creditors cannot piggyback on the Paulian action without their own proceedings.
common_disputes: Whether debtor's knowledge of harm to creditors is proved.
Whether the acquirer in an onerous transaction knew of debtor's fraud.
Scope of indirect action — which of debtor's rights can the creditor exercise?
practical_examples: Debtor donates property to relative while insolvent: Paulian action — donation ineffective as to creditor.
Debtor fails to collect large receivable: creditor may sue the debtor's debtor via oblique action.

title: termination of continuing contracts — إنهاء عقود المدة
content: Al-Sanhouri draws the fundamental distinction between instantaneous contracts (عقد فوري) and continuing contracts (عقد مستمر). In continuing contracts, rescission for breach operates prospectively — the court cannot undo already-performed obligations. This is a major exception to the retroactivity principle. He also establishes that contracts of indefinite duration can always be terminated unilaterally with reasonable notice — otherwise they would constitute an unlawful perpetual bond on freedom. The notice period must be reasonable under the circumstances, and termination in bad faith may give rise to damages even if formally valid.

metadata.source: Al-Sanhouri, Al-Wasit fi Sharh al-Qanun al-Madani (vol.1)

source_fields.topic: termination of continuing contracts — إنهاء عقود المدة
core_principles: Continuing contracts (عقود مستمرة) are those where performance unfolds over time — as opposed to instantaneous contracts.
Fixed-term contracts expire automatically at term without notice.
Indefinite-term contracts may be terminated unilaterally by either party with reasonable notice.
Rescission (فسخ) in continuing contracts is generally prospective only — not retroactive.

sanhouri_position.short: Continuing contracts have prospective rescission only — past performances cannot be unwound. Indefinite-term contracts may always be terminated with notice; no party can be bound in perpetuity. Reasonable notice requirement protects against abusive termination.

In continuing contracts, rescission for breach operates prospectively — the court cannot undo already-performed obligations. This is a major exception to the retroactivity principle. conditions: Continuing contract: performance extends over time (lease, employment, supply, partnership).
For indefinite term: unilateral termination valid with reasonable advance notice.
For fixed term: automatic expiry; renewal by parties' subsequent conduct may create indefinite continuation.
exceptions: Termination in bad faith even with notice: entitled to damages.
Tacit renewal: continuation after expiry of fixed term may create new indefinite contract.
Consumer protection laws may impose additional notice requirements in specific contracts.
effects: Prospective effect only: past performances stand.
No restitution of past performance (unlike instantaneous contract rescission).
Damages available for losses caused by the breach or abusive termination.
common_disputes: Whether notice was 'reasonable' in the circumstances.
Abusive termination of commercial agency or distribution agreements.
Whether termination of fixed-term contract before expiry requires compensation.
practical_examples: Supplier terminates indefinite supply agreement with 30-day notice: valid if notice is reasonable.
Franchisor terminates franchise agreement without adequate notice: abusive — damages due.

title: good faith in performance — حسن النية في تنفيذ الالتزامات
content: Al-Sanhouri treats Article 148 as one of the most productive general clauses of the Egyptian Code. Good faith in performance generates ancillary obligations not expressly stated: the duty to give information the other party needs to benefit from performance; the duty of cooperation to facilitate the other party's performance; the duty to mitigate avoidable damages. These are implied contract terms derived from good faith, custom, equity, and law — not from the parties' express agreement. He distinguishes good faith in performance (Article 148) from good faith as a defense protecting reliance (which appears elsewhere in the Code).

source_fields.topic: good faith in performance — حسن النية في تنفيذ الالتزامات
core_principles: Debtor must perform obligations in good faith and in accordance with their requirements (Article 148).
Good faith generates implied ancillary obligations: duty to inform, duty of loyalty, duty to mitigate.
Good faith in execution supplements but does not override express contractual terms.
Court may derive implied obligations from good faith, custom, equity, and law.

sanhouri_position.short: Good faith (Article 148) is a general clause generating implied performance obligations beyond express terms. Al-Sanhouri treats it as a source of ancillary duties (disclosure, cooperation, mitigation) that supplement the contract's express content.

Good faith in performance generates ancillary obligations not expressly stated: the duty to give information the other party needs to benefit from performance; the duty of cooperation to facilitate the other party's performance; the duty to mitigate avoidable damages. These are implied contract terms derived from good faith, custom, equity, and law — not from the parties' express agreement. conditions: Existing valid contractual obligation.
Ancillary duty arises when good faith, custom, equity, or law so requires.
Implied obligation must be consistent with the contract's nature and purpose.
exceptions: Good faith cannot override clear express terms — it supplements, not overrides.
Agreed allocation of risk expressly in contract: good faith does not shift it.
Commercial context: good faith standard may be more limited than in consumer contracts.
effects: Breach of implied good faith obligation creates contractual liability.
Court may refuse to enforce rights exercised in bad faith (abuse of contract rights).
Disclosure obligation: failure to disclose material facts may create liability.
common_disputes: Scope of implied disclosure obligation in specific transaction types.
Whether creditor's insistence on strict compliance is an abuse of contractual rights.
Duty of cooperation in construction and service contracts.
practical_examples: Seller failing to inform buyer of known latent defect not visible on inspection: bad faith breach.
Creditor refusing to accept performance for technical reason while debtor is in good faith: bad faith exercise of contract right.
